sources.name: CFPB, An essential guide to building an emergency fund
Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (executive summary)

facts.text: An emergency fund is a cash reserve set aside for unplanned expenses or financial emergencies, such as car repairs, home repairs, medical bills, or a loss of income.
How much you need depends on your situation. Think about the most common unexpected expenses you have had and what they cost to set a goal. Even a small amount can provide some financial security.

Without savings, even a minor financial shock can set you back, and if it turns into debt it can have a lasting impact. People with less savings may rely on credit cards or loans, which can lead to debt that is harder to pay off.
If you use a credit card or take out a loan to pay for an emergency expense, the bill can grow significantly larger than the original because of interest and fees.

Ways to build the fund include setting a specific goal, setting up automatic recurring transfers from checking to savings, saving all or part of a tax refund, and splitting your paycheck between two accounts through direct deposit.
Keep the fund safe, accessible, and somewhere you are not tempted to spend it on non-emergencies. A bank or credit union account is generally considered one of the safest places to keep money.

63 percent of adults said they would cover a hypothetical $400 emergency expense using cash, savings, or a credit card paid off at the next statement. This was unchanged from the previous three years, but down from a high of 68 percent in 2021.
